concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Lactate, tissue hypoxia, erythrocyte ATP, and the 2,3-BPG shunt
concepts.summary: Lactate dehydrogenase preserves glycolytic NAD+ during anaerobiosis; erythrocytes additionally divert 1,3-BPG through a 2,3-BPG shunt that trades ATP for oxygen-delivery control.
keyPoints: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and oxidizes NADH to NAD+, sustaining GAPDH when mitochondrial NADH reoxidation is unavailable.
Anaerobic glycolysis yields two ATP per glucose and no net NADH when glucose is converted to two lactate.
Hypoxic tissues, exercising muscle, RBCs, renal medulla, lens, cornea, and testes commonly produce lactate; liver can recycle lactate carbon through the Cori cycle.
RBC bisphosphoglycerate mutase converts 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG; 2,3-BPG phosphatase then yields 3-phosphoglycerate, bypassing phosphoglycerate kinase and sacrificing an ATP-forming opportunity.
The Chapter 8 source states that RBC 2,3-BPG increases oxygen delivery; diversion through the shunt therefore trades glycolytic ATP formation for oxygen-delivery control.
Lactate formation does not create extra ATP directly; its essential role is redox regeneration so ATP-producing glycolysis can continue.
The RBC 2,3-BPG shunt modifies oxygen delivery at an energetic cost by bypassing phosphoglycerate kinase.
examTraps: Lactate formation consumes NADH rather than producing it.
2,3-BPG is not the same as 1,3-BPG and its shunt bypasses an ATP-forming reaction.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the redox purpose of lactate formation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Regenerate NAD+ from NADH for GAPDH.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the energetic and physiologic effect of the RBC 2,3-BPG shunt?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It bypasses phosphoglycerate kinase and forfeits ATP formation while increasing oxygen delivery.

objectives.text: Explain lactate formation, tissue dependence on anaerobic glycolysis, and its net ATP/redox balance.
Predict how diversion through the erythrocyte 2,3-BPG shunt changes ATP yield and oxygen affinity.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glucose trapping: hexokinases, glucokinase, and GKRP
concepts.summary: The first glycolytic reaction traps glucose as glucose 6-phosphate; tissue-specific isoenzymes give distinct kinetics and regulation.
keyPoints: Hexokinases I-III have low Km, operate near saturation at normal glucose, occur in most tissues, and are inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate.
Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) occurs in hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells, has high Km and high Vmax, and is not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate.
Hepatic glucokinase processes a postprandial glucose load; pancreatic glucokinase acts as a glucose sensor for insulin secretion.
Glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP) sequesters glucokinase in the nucleus when fructose 6-phosphate is high; glucose and fructose 1-phosphate favor release to cytosol.
Glucokinase expression rises with insulin, and inactivating glucokinase mutations cause MODY2 with impaired insulin secretion.
The phosphate adds charge, preventing glucose 6-phosphate from leaving through GLUTs and directing it into glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, or the pentose phosphate pathway.
Glucokinase's high Km is physiologic: liver removes glucose efficiently only when portal glucose is high, preserving glucose for other tissues during fasting.
examTraps: High Km means lower affinity, not lower catalytic capacity.
Glucokinase is regulated by GKRP and enzyme abundance, not feedback inhibition by glucose 6-phosphate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do hexokinase and glucokinase differ after a carbohydrate meal?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Most hexokinases are already near saturation and can be inhibited by G6P; hepatic glucokinase remains responsive to high glucose and has high capacity.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What releases hepatic glucokinase from GKRP?
retrievalPrompts.answer: High glucose and fructose 1-phosphate favor its cytosolic release; fructose 6-phosphate favors nuclear sequestration.

objectives.text: Explain glucose trapping and compare the kinetics, tissues, and regulation of hexokinase I-III and glucokinase.
Predict glucokinase localization and activity from glucose, fructose metabolites, insulin, or GKRP.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: GLUT isoforms and sodium–monosaccharide cotransport
concepts.summary: Glucose crosses membranes through tissue-specific facilitated transporters or secondary active sodium cotransport.
keyPoints: GLUT1 supports basal uptake in many tissues and is prominent in RBCs and the blood-brain barrier; GLUT3 is the primary neuronal glucose transporter.
GLUT2 supports bidirectional glucose movement in liver and kidney and is also abundant in pancreatic beta cells.
GLUT4 is insulin responsive in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue; insulin recruits stored transporter vesicles to the plasma membrane.
GLUT5 primarily transports fructose in the small intestine and testes.
SGLT couples glucose uptake to inward sodium movement in intestine and renal tubule; the sodium gradient is maintained by Na+/K+-ATPase.
Facilitated transport follows a concentration gradient and does not directly hydrolyze ATP; SGLT is secondary active because ATP is spent indirectly to maintain the sodium gradient.
Transport and phosphorylation are distinct control points: GLUT entry precedes intracellular trapping as glucose 6-phosphate.
examTraps: GLUT2 is not insulin recruited.
SGLT does not itself hydrolyze ATP; the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase supplies the driving force.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Match GLUT1/2/3/4/5 to their defining tissues or substrates.
retrievalPrompts.answer: GLUT1 basal/RBC-BBB; GLUT2 bidirectional liver/kidney and pancreatic beta cell; GLUT3 neurons; GLUT4 insulin-responsive muscle/adipose; GLUT5 fructose.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is intestinal glucose uptake called secondary active transport?
retrievalPrompts.answer: SGLT couples glucose uphill transport to sodium downhill entry, whose gradient is created by Na+/K+-ATPase.

objectives.text: Differentiate GLUT isoforms by principal substrate, tissue distribution, transport direction, and insulin response.
Explain sodium-dependent intestinal/renal monosaccharide uptake and its energy source.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glycolysis overview, phases, products, and redox context
concepts.summary: Cytosolic glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate or lactate, producing ATP and intermediates in every tissue without directly requiring oxygen.
keyPoints: Glycolysis is cytosolic and universal; it supplies ATP plus intermediates for other pathways.
The first five reactions invest 2 ATP and split the hexose into two trioses; the payoff phase produces 4 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose, for a net 2 ATP.
With mitochondrial oxidative capacity, pyruvate is the principal product and cytosolic NADH is reoxidized through shuttles; without it, lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+.
Mature erythrocytes depend completely on anaerobic glycolysis because they lack mitochondria.
The term aerobic glycolysis describes the glycolytic pathway when mitochondrial reoxidation of NADH and pyruvate oxidation are available; molecular oxygen is not a glycolytic substrate.
Count payoff products per glucose, not per triose: all reactions after aldolase occur twice.
examTraps: Four ATP are formed gross, but two were invested, so the net is two.
NADH must be reoxidized; adequate oxygen alone cannot substitute for missing mitochondria.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the net glycolytic yield per glucose before pyruvate oxidation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Two pyruvate, two ATP net, two NADH, and two water.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can RBCs sustain glycolysis without mitochondria?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lactate dehydrogenase reoxidizes NADH to NAD+, allowing the GAPDH step to continue.

objectives.text: Compare aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis and identify tissues dependent on each context.
Calculate investment, gross payoff, and net ATP/NADH products per glucose.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Hepatic hormonal control and alternate fates of pyruvate
concepts.summary: Insulin and glucagon regulate hepatic glycolysis over short and long time scales, while pyruvate connects glycolysis to acetyl-CoA, oxaloacetate, lactate, and alanine.
keyPoints: In liver, insulin favors dephosphorylation of the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme, raising fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and glycolysis; glucagon/PKA phosphorylation produces the opposite effect.
Glucagon-mediated phosphorylation inhibits liver pyruvate kinase, conserving phosphoenolpyruvate for gluconeogenesis; insulin favors the active dephosphorylated form.
Insulin increases transcription of glucokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase; glucagon decreases expression of these glycolytic enzymes.
Pyruvate may undergo oxidative decarboxylation to acetyl-CoA, carboxylation to oxaloacetate, reduction to lactate, or transamination to alanine.
Coordinate liver pathways reciprocally: the same fasting signal that suppresses glycolysis should favor gluconeogenesis.
Pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA is irreversible in humans; acetyl-CoA therefore cannot yield net glucose through reversal of PDH.
examTraps: The phosphorylation response described is liver-specific; muscle PFK-2 and pyruvate kinase regulation differ.
Alanine formation is transamination, not decarboxylation.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does glucagon do to hepatic PFK-2/FBPase-2 and pyruvate kinase?
retrievalPrompts.answer: PKA phosphorylation lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and inhibits liver pyruvate kinase, suppressing glycolysis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: List four major fates of pyruvate.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Acetyl-CoA, oxaloacetate, lactate, and alanine.

objectives.text: Predict hepatic glycolytic flux from insulin/glucagon effects on PFK-2/FBPase-2, pyruvate kinase, and enzyme expression.
Select a pyruvate fate from tissue, oxygen, hormonal, or biosynthetic context.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Intracellular regulation and hormone–second-messenger signaling
concepts.summary: Flux is coordinated by substrate availability, allostery, covalent modification, enzyme amount, and intercellular signals relayed through receptors and second messengers.
keyPoints: Intracellular control includes substrate concentration, allosteric effectors, reversible covalent modification, and changes in enzyme synthesis or degradation.
Intercellular control uses hormones and neurotransmitters; cell-surface receptors are required for signals that do not cross the membrane.
Ligand-bound GPCR promotes GDP-to-GTP exchange on G-alpha; G-alpha-GTP separates from beta-gamma and regulates an effector such as adenylyl cyclase.
Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP, which activates protein kinase A; G-alpha hydrolyzes GTP to terminate the signal.
Cholera toxin locks Gs alpha active and raises cAMP; pertussis toxin prevents Gi alpha activation, removing inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and also raising cAMP in affected cells.
Separate rapid control (allostery and phosphorylation, seconds to minutes) from altered enzyme amount (hours to days). Both can change pathway flux.
A signaling cascade amplifies information: one occupied receptor can activate multiple G proteins, and each effector can generate many second-messenger molecules.
examTraps: GDP-bound G-alpha is inactive; GTP binding, not phosphorylation, activates it.
Pertussis toxin does not directly activate Gs; it inactivates Gi, so inhibitory input is lost.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What events connect ligand binding to PKA activation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: GPCR activation, GDP–GTP exchange on G-alpha, effector activation, cAMP production, then cAMP binding to PKA regulatory subunits.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why do cholera and pertussis toxins both tend to increase cAMP?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Cholera fixes Gs in its active state, whereas pertussis prevents inhibitory Gi signaling.

objectives.text: Distinguish intracellular from intercellular mechanisms that regulate metabolic flux.
Predict cAMP signaling after GPCR activation or bacterial toxin modification of G proteins.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Metabolic pathways, maps, catabolism and anabolism
concepts.summary: Metabolism is organized into linked enzyme-catalyzed pathways; catabolism is convergent and energy yielding, whereas anabolism is divergent and energy requiring.
keyPoints: In a pathway, the product of one enzyme-catalyzed reaction becomes the substrate for the next; pathways may be linear, branched, or cyclic.

Catabolism degrades dietary or stored macromolecules and captures chemical energy as ATP and reduced coenzymes; its three stages are hydrolysis to building blocks, conversion to acetyl-CoA, and oxidation of acetyl-CoA.
NAD+ and FAD accept electrons in oxidative catabolism; their reduced forms ultimately support ATP formation through oxidative phosphorylation.
Anabolism builds complex products from a small precursor pool, consumes ATP, and commonly uses NADPH as a reductant.
Metabolic maps emphasize convergence of carbohydrate, lipid, and amino-acid carbon on acetyl-CoA and the TCA cycle, then divergence into biosynthesis.
Read pathway maps by following carbon, energy, and reducing equivalents separately. Carbon convergence does not mean that every tissue performs every reaction.
The first catabolic stage releases monomers with little energy capture; most usable energy is captured after acetyl-CoA enters the TCA/respiratory system.
examTraps: Catabolic does not mean every individual step produces ATP.
NADPH is the characteristic biosynthetic reductant; NADH is the major oxidative-catabolic electron carrier.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Name the three stages of catabolism.
retrievalPrompts.answer: Hydrolysis of complex molecules, conversion of building blocks to acetyl-CoA, and oxidation of acetyl-CoA to CO2 with electron transfer and ATP production.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why are catabolism and anabolism described as convergent and divergent?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Many fuels converge on a few products such as acetyl-CoA, whereas a few precursors diverge into many complex products.

objectives.text: Classify pathways and contrast catabolic with anabolic organization, energy use, and reducing cofactors.
Reconstruct the three stages of fuel catabolism and locate acetyl-CoA/TCA as the convergence point.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glycolytic payoff reactions and substrate-level phosphorylation
concepts.summary: Oxidation of two glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate molecules supplies NADH and high-energy intermediates that drive four ATP-forming events per glucose.
keyPoints: GAPDH oxidizes glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and adds inorganic phosphate to form 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate while NAD+ becomes NADH.
Phosphoglycerate kinase transfers phosphate from 1,3-BPG to ADP; this reversible step is the first substrate-level phosphorylation.
Phosphoglycerate mutase moves phosphate from carbon 3 to carbon 2; enolase dehydrates 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate.
Fluoride inhibits enolase, which is why fluoride-containing blood tubes slow glycolysis in collected samples.
Pyruvate kinase irreversibly transfers PEP phosphate to ADP; fructose 1,6-bisphosphate feed-forward activates the enzyme, while hepatic phosphorylation inhibits the liver isozyme.
Substrate-level phosphorylation forms ATP by direct phosphate transfer; it does not require the electron-transport chain.
Both ATP-forming steps occur twice per glucose. The GAPDH step requires continuously available NAD+.
examTraps: Phosphoglycerate kinase is reversible despite producing ATP.
Enolase makes PEP; pyruvate kinase consumes PEP.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Trace the payoff phase from glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate to pyruvate.
retrievalPrompts.answer: GAPDH → phosphoglycerate kinase → phosphoglycerate mutase → enolase → pyruvate kinase.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which glycolytic reactions make ATP directly?
retrievalPrompts.answer: 1,3-BPG to 3-phosphoglycerate and PEP to pyruvate.

objectives.text: Connect GAPDH redox chemistry to the two substrate-level phosphorylation steps and final pyruvate formation.
Recognize pharmacologic/collection inhibition of enolase and the biochemical consequence.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: PFK-1 commitment, reciprocal regulation, aldolase, and triose isomerase
concepts.summary: PFK-1 commits glucose to glycolysis; aldolase and triose phosphate isomerase then convert one hexose into two metabolizable glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate molecules.
keyPoints: Phosphoglucose isomerase reversibly converts glucose 6-phosphate to fructose 6-phosphate, preparing the carbonyl position for symmetric cleavage later.
PFK-1 converts fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and is the committed, rate-limiting glycolytic step.
ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1; AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate activate it.
Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate simultaneously activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, coordinating glycolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Aldolase yields glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and DHAP; triose phosphate isomerase converts DHAP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate so both three-carbon products continue through glycolysis.
Commitment is not the same as the first reaction. Glucose 6-phosphate has multiple fates; fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is committed to glycolysis.
PFK-1 integrates energy state (ATP/AMP), biosynthetic sufficiency (citrate), and hepatic hormonal state (fructose 2,6-bisphosphate).
examTraps: PFK-2 makes fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; PFK-1 uses fructose 6-phosphate as substrate.
Aldolase does not yield two glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate directly.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which signals inhibit and activate PFK-1?
retrievalPrompts.answer: ATP and citrate inhibit; AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate activate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is triose phosphate isomerase required?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Only glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate proceeds directly, so DHAP must be isomerized to obtain two payoff-phase streams per glucose.

objectives.text: Identify the committed glycolytic step and predict PFK-1 flux from its major effectors.
Trace carbon through phosphoglucose isomerase, aldolase, and triose phosphate isomerase.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and succinyl-CoA synthetase
concepts.summary: The second oxidative decarboxylation forms succinyl-CoA, whose thioester energy is captured as GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
keyPoints: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase yields succinyl-CoA, CO2, and NADH and uses the same five coenzymes as PDH.
Its activity is inhibited by NADH and succinyl-CoA and activated by Ca2+ in muscle; the reaction is irreversible.
Succinyl-CoA synthetase (succinate thiokinase) converts succinyl-CoA to succinate and produces GTP from GDP and Pi.
Nucleoside diphosphate kinase can convert GTP + ADP to GDP + ATP, making the energy equivalent interchangeable.
Succinyl-CoA is also a precursor for heme synthesis and receives carbon from propionyl-CoA metabolism.
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase mirrors PDH in reaction logic: oxidative decarboxylation of an alpha-keto acid by a multienzyme complex.
This is the only TCA substrate-level phosphorylation; all other energy is captured first as NADH or FADH2.
examTraps: Succinyl-CoA synthetase makes GTP, not reduced coenzyme.
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase does not use biotin.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which TCA enzyme shares all five PDH cofactors?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does succinyl-CoA yield an ATP equivalent?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Succinyl-CoA synthetase makes GTP, which nucleoside diphosphate kinase can exchange with ATP.

objectives.text: Explain alpha-ketoglutarate oxidative decarboxylation, cofactor use, and regulation.
Identify the succinyl-CoA synthetase step as TCA substrate-level phosphorylation and connect succinyl-CoA to heme/propionate.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Citrate synthase, aconitase, and isocitrate dehydrogenase
concepts.summary: The first oxidative segment condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate, rearranges citrate, then performs the first oxidative decarboxylation.
keyPoints: Citrate synthase irreversibly condenses acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate; hydrolysis of the thioester drives citrate formation.
Aconitase reversibly isomerizes citrate to isocitrate through cis-aconitate; fluorocitrate inhibits aconitase after fluoroacetate intoxication.
Isocitrate dehydrogenase forms alpha-ketoglutarate, CO2, and NADH and is a major regulated TCA step.
ADP and Ca2+ activate isocitrate dehydrogenase; ATP and NADH inhibit it.
Citrate export carries acetyl units for cytosolic fatty-acid/cholesterol synthesis and citrate also inhibits PFK-1.
The two carbons lost in the first turn are not necessarily the newly entered acetyl carbons because of molecular rearrangement and cycle symmetry.
Citrate is both a cycle intermediate and a signal of abundant carbon/energy.
examTraps: Aconitase does not decarboxylate citrate.
Ca2+ activation supports contracting muscle energy demand; citrate synthase is not the only regulated enzyme.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the products of isocitrate dehydrogenase?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Alpha-ketoglutarate, CO2, and NADH.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does exported citrate communicate and supply?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It signals abundant energy, inhibits PFK-1, and supplies cytosolic acetyl units for lipid synthesis.

objectives.text: Trace acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate through citrate, isocitrate, and alpha-ketoglutarate with enzymes and redox products.
Recognize citrate export and fluorocitrate inhibition as pathway integrations.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: TCA-cycle convergence, amphibolic function, and anaplerosis
concepts.summary: The mitochondrial TCA cycle is the final common oxidative pathway for acetyl-CoA and an amphibolic hub whose intermediates must be replenished when withdrawn.
keyPoints: Carbohydrate, fatty-acid, and many amino-acid carbon skeletons converge on acetyl-CoA and the TCA cycle, where acetyl carbon is oxidized to CO2.
The cycle is aerobic indirectly: oxygen is not a substrate, but NADH and FADH2 require the respiratory chain and oxygen for reoxidation.
The cycle is amphibolic because it supports both catabolism and biosynthesis; citrate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, and oxaloacetate are withdrawn for synthetic pathways.
Anaplerotic reactions replenish intermediates. The major human example is biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase producing oxaloacetate.
Except for succinate dehydrogenase in the inner membrane, mammalian TCA enzymes reside in the mitochondrial matrix; mature RBCs cannot run the cycle.
Acetyl-CoA carbon entry does not cause net accumulation of intermediates because oxaloacetate is regenerated; withdrawal must be balanced by anaplerosis.
A pathway can be oxygen dependent even if none of its enzymes binds O2 directly.
examTraps: Acetyl-CoA is not itself an anaplerotic substrate because its two carbons are balanced by CO2 loss.
RBCs lack the entire mitochondrial context, not just one TCA enzyme.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is the TCA cycle both final common pathway and amphibolic hub?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It oxidizes acetyl-CoA from all major fuels while supplying intermediates for biosynthesis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What reaction is the major anaplerotic source of oxaloacetate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → oxaloacetate.

objectives.text: Explain convergence, indirect oxygen dependence, compartmentation, and RBC exclusion from the TCA cycle.
Distinguish cataplerotic withdrawal from anaplerotic replenishment and identify pyruvate carboxylase.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: PDH irreversible chemistry, enzyme components, and five coenzymes
concepts.summary: The mitochondrial PDH complex irreversibly links glycolysis to acetyl-CoA through coordinated decarboxylation, oxidation, and acetyl transfer.
keyPoints: The net reaction is pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH; it is irreversible and occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
E1 pyruvate dehydrogenase uses thiamine pyrophosphate; E2 dihydrolipoyl transacetylase uses lipoamide and transfers the acetyl group to CoA.
E3 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase reoxidizes reduced lipoamide using FAD, then transfers electrons to NAD+.
The five coenzymes are TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+; all except lipoate are vitamin derived.
Physical clustering permits substrate channeling, minimizes loss of reactive intermediates, and coordinates regulation.
Use the mnemonic sequence TPP–lipoate–CoA–FAD–NAD+, but also understand which E component uses each cofactor.
PDH removes one carbon as CO2, retains two in acetyl-CoA, and captures electrons as NADH.
examTraps: PDH does not generate ATP directly.
FAD is enzyme bound at E3; NAD+ is the final mobile electron acceptor.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Match E1, E2, and E3 to their core tasks.
retrievalPrompts.answer: E1 decarboxylates pyruvate with TPP; E2 transfers the acetyl group through lipoate to CoA; E3 reoxidizes lipoate via FAD and NAD+.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is PDH a metabolic point of no return for glucose carbon?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Its oxidative decarboxylation is physiologically irreversible, so acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate.

objectives.text: State the PDH net reaction, location, irreversibility, and five required coenzymes.
Assign the sequential catalytic roles and cofactors of E1, E2, and E3.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: PDH covalent regulation, deficiency, thiamine, and arsenic
concepts.summary: PDH is switched off by E1 phosphorylation and on by dephosphorylation; energy signals, Ca2+, enzyme defects, and cofactor toxins determine pyruvate flux.
keyPoints: PDH kinase phosphorylates and inactivates E1; it is stimulated by ATP, NADH, and acetyl-CoA and inhibited by pyruvate.
PDH phosphatase dephosphorylates and activates E1; Ca2+ activates it in contracting skeletal muscle, and insulin stimulates it in adipose tissue.
E1 deficiency is the most common biochemical cause of congenital lactic acidosis; pyruvate is diverted to lactate, often causing neurologic injury.
Thiamine deficiency impairs TPP-dependent PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and can contribute to lactic acidosis.
Arsenite binds reduced lipoic acid sulfhydryls and inhibits PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
High-energy product signals inhibit further acetyl-CoA formation. During contraction, Ca2+ coordinates PDH activation with increased TCA demand.
The cited chapter describes carbohydrate restriction and thiamine supplementation as potentially reducing symptoms in selected PDH-deficient patients, while noting that no treatment is proven.
examTraps: Phosphorylation inactivates PDH, the opposite of glycogen phosphorylase.
Arsenite targets lipoate; fluoroacetate targets aconitase after conversion to fluorocitrate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What combination activates PDH during muscle contraction?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Ca2+ activates PDH phosphatase, which dephosphorylates and activates E1.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why do PDH deficiency and thiamine deficiency raise lactate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Both reduce pyruvate oxidation, increasing pyruvate availability for lactate dehydrogenase.

objectives.text: Predict PDH activity from kinase/phosphatase action, energy signals, pyruvate, Ca2+, and insulin.
Recognize PDH/thiamine/arsenite mechanisms from a lactic-acidosis or toxin vignette.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Succinate oxidation, fumarate hydration, and oxaloacetate regeneration
concepts.summary: The final three reactions restore oxaloacetate while transferring one electron pair to FAD and one to NAD+.
keyPoints: Succinate dehydrogenase is TCA enzyme and respiratory Complex II; it is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and reduces FAD to FADH2 while making fumarate.
Electrons from enzyme-bound FADH2 pass to coenzyme Q and bypass Complex I.
Fumarase stereospecifically hydrates fumarate to L-malate.
Malate dehydrogenase oxidizes malate to oxaloacetate while producing NADH; the unfavorable reaction is pulled forward by citrate synthase consumption of oxaloacetate.
Complex II is the structural exception among TCA enzymes and the respiratory-chain exception that does not pump protons.
Coupled pathway flux can drive an individually unfavorable reaction by removing its product.
examTraps: Succinate dehydrogenase makes FADH2, not NADH.
Fumarase adds water; aconitase is the citrate/isocitrate isomerase.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which enzyme links the TCA cycle directly to the respiratory chain?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Succinate dehydrogenase/Complex II.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can malate oxidation proceed in vivo despite a positive standard free-energy change?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Oxaloacetate is kept low by citrate synthase, pulling the reaction forward.

objectives.text: Trace succinate to oxaloacetate with enzymes, cofactors, products, and compartment-specific features.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: TCA stoichiometry, ATP equivalents, and integrated regulation
concepts.summary: Each acetyl-CoA yields three NADH, one FADH2, one GTP, and two CO2; the cited sixth edition applies its own 3-ATP/NADH and 2-ATP/FADH2 convention while regulated enzymes integrate energy and contraction signals.
keyPoints: One turn transfers four electron pairs: three to NAD+ and one to FAD; it also forms one GTP and releases two CO2.
Using the convention printed in this sixth-edition chapter, three NADH yield about 9 ATP, one FADH2 about 2 ATP, and GTP one ATP equivalent: 12 ATP equivalents per acetyl-CoA.
Citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase catalyze the major regulated irreversible steps.
High ATP and NADH suppress cycle flux; ADP and Ca2+ stimulate appropriate enzymes when energy demand rises.
Cycle rate also depends on acetyl-CoA/oxaloacetate availability and reoxidation of reduced coenzymes by the respiratory chain.
Stoichiometry per turn is fixed, but actual flux is controlled by energy charge, redox state, substrate supply, and downstream respiratory capacity.
For this source-bounded catalog, use the edition's printed 12-ATP convention; do not silently substitute a different P/O convention.

Oxygen affects the TCA cycle through NADH/FADH2 reoxidation, not as a direct substrate.
ATP-equivalent totals depend on the named P/O convention; this edition uses three per NADH and two per FADH2 in Chapter 9.

retrievalPrompts.answer: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, and 2 CO2.

retrievalPrompts.answer: ADP and Ca2+ activate regulated dehydrogenases while lower ATP/NADH relieves inhibition.

Predict TCA flux from ATP/ADP, NADH, Ca2+, substrate supply, and respiratory capacity.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Cori cycle and ethanol-induced hypoglycemia
concepts.summary: The Cori cycle returns lactate carbon to hepatic glucose, whereas ethanol-driven excess NADH blocks key precursor reactions and can cause fasting hypoglycemia.
keyPoints: In the Cori cycle, muscle or RBC lactate travels to liver, becomes glucose, and returns to peripheral tissues; the liver bears the energetic cost.
Interorgan lactate cycling shifts work rather than creating energy: peripheral tissues gain glycolytic ATP while liver spends energy to resynthesize glucose.
Ethanol oxidation raises hepatic NADH/NAD+, driving pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate.
Loss of pyruvate and oxaloacetate from gluconeogenesis can cause severe hypoglycemia during fasting, especially when glycogen is depleted.
Elevated lactate can accompany the high-reducing-state response.
The Cori cycle transports lactate carbon from peripheral tissue to liver and returns it as glucose.
Ethanol hypoglycemia is a redox problem, not direct inhibition of a single gluconeogenic enzyme.
examTraps: The Cori cycle transports lactate; alanine is separately a gluconeogenic amino acid in the cited chapter.
A fed patient with adequate glycogen is less vulnerable to ethanol-associated hypoglycemia than a fasting patient.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does the Cori cycle accomplish?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It clears lactate and returns its carbon as hepatic glucose at an energy cost to liver.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does ethanol-derived NADH block gluconeogenesis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It shifts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, depleting gluconeogenic precursors.

objectives.text: Explain the carbon traffic and energetic purpose of the Cori cycle.
Recognize fasting ethanol-induced hypoglycemia from redox-driven pyruvate/lactate and oxaloacetate/malate shifts.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Energetic cost of gluconeogenesis
concepts.summary: Synthesis of one glucose from two pyruvate consumes four ATP, two GTP, and two NADH, making gluconeogenesis an energy-requiring pathway.
keyPoints: Two pyruvate carboxylase reactions consume 2 ATP and two PEPCK reactions consume 2 GTP.
Reversal of phosphoglycerate kinase consumes another 2 ATP; GAPDH reduction consumes 2 NADH.
The net cost is 4 ATP + 2 GTP + 2 NADH per glucose from two pyruvate, equivalent to six high-energy phosphate bonds plus reducing power.
Fatty-acid oxidation commonly supplies this energy during fasting.
Compare net glycolysis and gluconeogenesis rather than imagining exact reversal: the bypasses impose an extra energetic cost that prevents equilibrium cycling.
When lactate is the precursor, its oxidation supplies the two cytosolic NADH needed downstream.
examTraps: The cost is not just two ATP.
GTP is consumed by PEPCK, not generated as in the succinyl-CoA synthetase step.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is consumed to form glucose from two pyruvate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: 4 ATP, 2 GTP, and 2 NADH.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which reactions account for the six nucleotide triphosphates?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Two ATP at pyruvate carboxylase, two GTP at PEPCK, and two ATP at phosphoglycerate kinase reversal.

objectives.text: Calculate the ATP, GTP, and NADH cost of glucose synthesis from pyruvate and assign each cost to a reaction.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Oxaloacetate transport, cytosolic redox, and PEPCK
concepts.summary: Because oxaloacetate cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, malate or mitochondrial PEP export bridges compartments and helps balance cytosolic NADH.
keyPoints: PEPCK converts oxaloacetate + GTP to PEP + GDP + CO2 and exists in both mitochondrial and cytosolic forms in humans.
Oxaloacetate cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane; it is commonly reduced to malate, transported, and reoxidized in cytosol.
The malate route transfers reducing equivalents to cytosol, supplying NADH needed for gluconeogenesis from pyruvate or alanine.
When lactate is the precursor, cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase already generates NADH, so mitochondrial PEP can be exported directly.
Carboxylation followed by decarboxylation and GTP use drives formation of high-energy PEP.
Choose the export route by redox need: pyruvate/alanine requires the malate shuttle for cytosolic NADH; lactate supplies NADH during its own oxidation.
The bypass uses two enzymes and crosses compartments, unlike a simple reversal of pyruvate kinase.
examTraps: OAA is not transported directly across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
PEPCK decarboxylates and phosphorylates OAA; it does not consume ATP.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is mitochondrial OAA converted to malate during gluconeogenesis from pyruvate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: To permit carbon export and deliver cytosolic NADH.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How can the route differ when lactate is the precursor?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Cytosolic lactate oxidation supplies NADH, allowing mitochondrial OAA to become PEP and PEP to be exported.

objectives.text: Explain PEPCK chemistry and the two compartmental routes from mitochondrial oxaloacetate to cytosolic PEP.
Select the malate-versus-PEP export route based on the precursor's cytosolic NADH contribution.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase and ER glucose 6-phosphatase
concepts.summary: Two hydrolytic bypasses reverse the committed glycolytic phosphorylation and permit glucose release without synthesizing ATP.
keyPoints: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase hydrolyzes fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to fructose 6-phosphate in liver and kidney; AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate inhibit it.
Glucose 6-phosphatase hydrolyzes glucose 6-phosphate in the ER lumen of liver and kidney, allowing free glucose to leave the cell.
A glucose 6-phosphate translocase moves substrate into the ER; glucose and Pi products return to cytosol before glucose exits through GLUT2.
Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and therefore uses glycogen-derived glucose 6-phosphate locally.
The phosphatase reactions dissipate phosphate ester energy; they are not ATP-forming reversals of kinase steps.
The final reaction's ER topology is clinically important in glucose 6-phosphatase/translocase defects and distinguishes glucose-producing tissues.
Reciprocal regulation prevents PFK-1 and FBPase-1 from running strongly at the same time.
examTraps: FBPase-1 is not the bifunctional FBPase-2 domain.
Glucose 6-phosphatase is not a cytosolic muscle enzyme.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which glycolytic steps are bypassed by FBPase-1 and glucose 6-phosphatase?
retrievalPrompts.answer: PFK-1 and hexokinase/glucokinase, respectively.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does G6P reach glucose 6-phosphatase?
retrievalPrompts.answer: A translocase carries G6P into the ER lumen, where the phosphatase hydrolyzes it.

objectives.text: Identify FBPase-1 and glucose 6-phosphatase reactions, tissues, and reciprocal regulators.
Describe ER transport and hydrolysis in the terminal glucose-release system.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Physiologic purpose, fasting sequence, organs, and compartments
concepts.summary: Gluconeogenesis maintains circulating glucose after hepatic glycogen wanes, primarily in liver and increasingly in kidney cortex during prolonged fasting.
keyPoints: Glucose-dependent tissues include RBCs, renal medulla, lens/cornea, testes, and parts of the brain; exercising muscle also has high glucose demand.
Liver glycogen can support blood glucose for roughly 10-18 hours without carbohydrate intake; thereafter gluconeogenesis becomes essential.
Liver is the major early source; kidney cortex contributes substantially in prolonged fasting, whereas muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and does not export free glucose.
Reactions are distributed between mitochondrial matrix, cytosol, and endoplasmic reticulum rather than occurring in one compartment.
Gluconeogenesis begins before glycogen is completely exhausted and progressively assumes the dominant role.
Tissue location must be paired with subcellular location: liver/kidney are organs, whereas matrix/cytosol/ER describe reaction compartments.
examTraps: Renal medulla consumes glucose; renal cortex performs gluconeogenesis.
Skeletal muscle can make glucose 6-phosphate but cannot release free glucose to blood.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which organs maintain blood glucose during prolonged fasting?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Primarily liver and increasingly kidney cortex.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is gluconeogenesis compartmentally complex?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Pyruvate carboxylation is mitochondrial, many reversible reactions are cytosolic, and glucose 6-phosphatase functions in ER.

objectives.text: Explain when and why gluconeogenesis becomes essential and name glucose-dependent tissues.
Identify organ and subcellular sites and explain why muscle cannot export glucose.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Pyruvate carboxylase, biotin, and acetyl-CoA signaling
concepts.summary: Mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase uses ATP, bicarbonate, and biotin to generate oxaloacetate and is obligatorily activated by acetyl-CoA.
keyPoints: Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial biotin-dependent enzyme: pyruvate + HCO3- + ATP → oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi.
Biotin carries activated CO2 through a covalent linkage to a lysine residue in pyruvate carboxylase.
Acetyl-CoA is an obligatory allosteric activator, signaling that pyruvate should replenish oxaloacetate or support gluconeogenesis rather than form more acetyl-CoA.
During fasting, fatty-acid oxidation supplies ATP/NADH and raises acetyl-CoA, activating pyruvate carboxylase while inhibiting PDH.
The CO2 added by pyruvate carboxylase is later removed by PEPCK; carboxylation provides the thermodynamic strategy to bypass irreversible pyruvate kinase.
Pyruvate carboxylase serves both anaplerosis and gluconeogenesis; context determines the fate of oxaloacetate.
examTraps: PEPCK uses GTP; pyruvate carboxylase uses ATP.
Biotin carries CO2, whereas TPP supports alpha-ketoacid decarboxylation.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the substrates, products, cofactor, and activator of pyruvate carboxylase?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Pyruvate, bicarbonate, and ATP form oxaloacetate; biotin is the cofactor and acetyl-CoA is the obligatory activator.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does fatty-acid oxidation promote pyruvate carboxylation?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It supplies ATP and acetyl-CoA, which activates pyruvate carboxylase and inhibits PDH.

objectives.text: Specify pyruvate-carboxylase chemistry, location, cofactor, and allosteric control.
Explain how fatty-acid oxidation reciprocally directs pyruvate away from PDH and toward oxaloacetate.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glucagon, fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, substrate supply, and gene regulation
concepts.summary: Fasting increases hepatic gluconeogenesis by lowering fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, increasing substrate/energy supply, and changing enzyme expression.
keyPoints: Glucagon raises cAMP/PKA, phosphorylating hepatic PFK-2/FBPase-2 so FBPase-2 activity predominates and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate falls.
Low fructose 2,6-bisphosphate inhibits PFK-1 and relieves FBPase-1 inhibition, reciprocally favoring gluconeogenesis.
High AMP inhibits FBPase-1, preventing an energy-consuming pathway when cellular energy is low.
Low insulin promotes muscle proteolysis and adipose lipolysis, supplying amino-acid carbon, glycerol, ATP, NADH, and acetyl-CoA.
Glucagon increases PEPCK and other gluconeogenic enzyme expression; insulin has opposing transcriptional effects.
Moment-to-moment control is dominated by glucagon and substrate availability; gene-expression effects reinforce the fasting program over hours.
Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase and inhibits PDH, while fatty-acid oxidation provides the required energy.
examTraps: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a regulator, not a gluconeogenic intermediate.
Glucagon acts directly on liver, not skeletal muscle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does glucagon change fructose 2,6-bisphosphate?
retrievalPrompts.answer: PKA phosphorylation shifts the bifunctional enzyme toward FBPase-2, lowering fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does low insulin provide both carbon and energy for gluconeogenesis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Proteolysis supplies glucogenic amino acids; lipolysis supplies glycerol and fatty acids whose oxidation supplies ATP/NADH/acetyl-CoA.

objectives.text: Predict reciprocal glycolysis/gluconeogenesis from glucagon, insulin, AMP, and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
Explain how substrate mobilization, fatty-acid oxidation, and enzyme expression sustain fasting gluconeogenesis.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Gluconeogenic precursors and carbon-entry logic
concepts.summary: Lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids enter at pyruvate, DHAP, or TCA intermediates; even-chain fatty acids cannot provide net glucose.
keyPoints: Lactate becomes pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase and participates in the Cori cycle; alanine becomes pyruvate by transamination and serves as an important glucogenic amino-acid precursor.
Glycerol from adipose TAG becomes glycerol 3-phosphate and then DHAP in liver, which has glycerol kinase.
Glucogenic amino-acid carbon enters as pyruvate or TCA intermediates; leucine and lysine are exclusively ketogenic.
Even-chain fatty-acid acetyl-CoA cannot yield net glucose because PDH is irreversible and TCA acetyl carbons are lost as CO2 without net oxaloacetate gain.
Odd-chain fatty acids yield propionyl-CoA, then succinyl-CoA, providing a gluconeogenic route.
A precursor is gluconeogenic only if its carbon can produce net oxaloacetate or a glycolytic intermediate, not merely enter the TCA cycle as acetyl-CoA.
Glycerol is the TAG component that yields net glucose; most fatty-acid carbon does not.
examTraps: Acetyl-CoA activates gluconeogenesis but is not itself a net glucose carbon source.
Lactate-to-pyruvate requires NAD+ and is inhibited by a high hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where do lactate, alanine, and glycerol enter?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Lactate and alanine enter as pyruvate; glycerol enters as DHAP.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why are odd-chain but not even-chain fatty acids glucogenic?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Odd-chain oxidation yields propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA; even-chain oxidation yields only acetyl-CoA.

objectives.text: Route lactate, alanine, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids into gluconeogenesis.
Use net-carbon accounting to distinguish even- and odd-chain fatty-acid contributions.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Allosteric control in liver/muscle and Ca2+-calmodulin activation
concepts.summary: Local energy and glucose signals modify glycogen enzymes independently of hormones, while contraction Ca2+ activates phosphorylase kinase through its calmodulin subunit.
keyPoints: Muscle phosphorylase b is allosterically activated by AMP and inhibited by ATP and glucose 6-phosphate, matching local energy need.
Liver phosphorylase a binds free glucose, shifts toward the inactive conformation, and becomes a better substrate for phosphatase.
Glucose 6-phosphate allosterically activates glycogen synthase b, favoring storage when intracellular glucose is abundant.
Phosphorylase kinase contains a calmodulin delta subunit; Ca2+ released during contraction partially activates it even without cAMP.
PKA phosphorylation and Ca2+ binding synergize to maximize phosphorylase kinase activity in exercising muscle.
Liver senses blood-glucose abundance; muscle senses its own energy charge. This explains different allosteric regulators despite shared enzymes.
Calcium couples excitation directly to fuel mobilization before hormonal signaling is required.
examTraps: AMP activates muscle phosphorylase, not liver glucose export.
Ca2+ binds the calmodulin subunit of phosphorylase kinase; it does not directly phosphorylate glycogen.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do AMP and glucose regulate muscle versus liver phosphorylase?
retrievalPrompts.answer: AMP activates muscle phosphorylase b; free glucose promotes inactivation of liver phosphorylase a.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does contraction activate glycogenolysis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Ca2+ binds calmodulin within phosphorylase kinase, which activates glycogen phosphorylase.

objectives.text: Differentiate liver and muscle allosteric regulation by glucose, AMP, ATP, and glucose 6-phosphate.
Explain Ca2+/calmodulin activation of phosphorylase kinase during contraction.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glycogen phosphorylase and glucose 1-phosphate production
concepts.summary: Cytosolic glycogenolysis uses phosphorolysis to conserve bond energy as glucose 1-phosphate until phosphorylase approaches a branch.
keyPoints: Glycogen phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate and pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) to cleave alpha-1,4 bonds at nonreducing ends.
The product is glucose 1-phosphate, conserving energy compared with hydrolytic release of free glucose.
Phosphorylase stops four residues from an alpha-1,6 branch, leaving a limit dextrin for debranching enzyme.
Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose 1-phosphate to glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis or, in liver, eventual blood-glucose release.
Phosphorylase a is phosphorylated and generally active; phosphorylase b is dephosphorylated and less active but can respond to AMP in muscle.
Phosphorolysis saves one ATP in muscle because G1P becomes G6P without hexokinase ATP use.
The PLP role here is acid–base catalysis involving phosphate, distinct from its aminotransferase role.
examTraps: Glycogen phosphorylase releases G1P, not G6P.
It cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds and cannot pass an alpha-1,6 branch.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is phosphorolysis energetically useful?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It releases phosphorylated glucose, bypassing ATP-dependent hexokinase after conversion to G6P.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where does phosphorylase stop?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Four residues from an alpha-1,6 branch, forming a limit dextrin.

objectives.text: Specify glycogen-phosphorylase substrate, bond, products, cofactor, and stopping point.
Explain how phosphoglucomutase routes glycogen-derived carbon toward tissue-specific fates.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Debranching enzyme and lysosomal glycogen degradation
concepts.summary: A bifunctional debranching enzyme resolves limit dextrin in cytosol, whereas a small independent fraction of glycogen is hydrolyzed in lysosomes by acid alpha-glucosidase.
keyPoints: The debranching transferase moves three residues from a four-residue stub to another chain, exposing the branch-point glucose.
Its alpha-1,6-glucosidase activity hydrolyzes the branch bond and releases free glucose, not glucose 1-phosphate.
After debranching, glycogen phosphorylase resumes alpha-1,4 phosphorolysis.
Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase independently hydrolyzes a small fraction of glycogen; its deficiency causes Pompe disease.
Debranching-enzyme deficiency causes limit-dextrin accumulation (Cori/Forbes disease).
One polypeptide contains two distinct debranching activities; their order matters: transfer first, then hydrolyze the exposed branch residue.
Lysosomal glycogen turnover is separate from the phosphorylase/debranching pathway and explains why Pompe disease is a lysosomal storage disorder.
examTraps: The branch-point residue is released as free glucose.
Pompe disease is not a cytosolic phosphorylase deficiency.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What two activities resolve a limit dextrin?
retrievalPrompts.answer: A 4-alpha-glucanotransferase moves three residues, then alpha-1,6-glucosidase releases the branch glucose.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which glycogen degradation defect is lysosomal?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency in Pompe disease.

objectives.text: Sequence the two debranching activities and identify the products.
Distinguish cytosolic glycogenolysis from lysosomal acid-alpha-glucosidase turnover.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glucagon/epinephrine cascades and reciprocal phosphorylation
concepts.summary: cAMP/PKA signaling activates glycogen breakdown and inhibits synthesis through a reciprocal phosphorylation cascade; insulin promotes protein-phosphatase-1 action.
keyPoints: Glucagon acts on liver but not skeletal muscle; epinephrine acts on both through appropriate adrenergic receptors.
Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cAMP–PKA signaling activates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase b to active a.
PKA also phosphorylates glycogen synthase to the less-active b form, preventing simultaneous synthesis.
Insulin activates protein phosphatase-1, which dephosphorylates glycogen synthase (activating it) and phosphorylase kinase/phosphorylase (inactivating them).
Phosphodiesterase terminates cAMP signaling; phosphatase action reverses the phosphorylation cascade.
Follow phosphorylation by target rather than memorizing one universal rule: it activates glycogen phosphorylase but inhibits glycogen synthase.
Hormone specificity depends on receptor expression; absence of glucagon receptors prevents direct muscle response.
examTraps: Insulin does not activate glycogen phosphorylase.
Glucagon is a hepatic fasting signal; muscle responds to epinephrine and contraction signals.

retrievalPrompts.answer: PKA activates the phosphorylase cascade while phosphorylating/inhibiting glycogen synthase.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does insulin reverse the fasting program?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Protein phosphatase-1 activates synthase by dephosphorylation and inactivates phosphorylase system components.

objectives.text: Trace glucagon/epinephrine from receptor to cAMP, PKA, phosphorylase kinase, and glycogen phosphorylase.
Predict reciprocal synthase/phosphorylase activity after PKA or protein phosphatase-1 action.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glycogen-storage diseases: enzyme–organ–structure patterns
concepts.summary: Glycogen-storage disorders are distinguished by the missing enzyme, organ distribution, abnormal glycogen structure, and fasting/exercise phenotype.
keyPoints: Von Gierke (type I), glucose 6-phosphatase system deficiency: severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.
Pompe (type II), lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency: cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, and lysosomal glycogen with generally normal structure.

Cori/Forbes (type III), debranching-enzyme deficiency: limit dextrin, hepatomegaly, and milder hypoglycemia; Andersen (type IV), branching-enzyme deficiency: long poorly soluble chains and progressive cirrhosis.
McArdle (type V), muscle phosphorylase deficiency: exercise intolerance/cramps, myoglobinuria, absent lactate rise, and possible second-wind phenomenon.
Hers (type VI), liver phosphorylase deficiency: generally mild fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.
Use a four-column matrix: enzyme, organelle/tissue, glycogen structure, and clinical trigger. This avoids confusing similarly numbered diseases.
Normal blood lactate after exercise points to failure to access muscle glycogen; severe fasting hypoglycemia points to hepatic glucose-release failure.
examTraps: Pompe is the only classic lysosomal glycogenosis in this chapter set.
Branching deficiency gives long outer chains; debranching deficiency gives short limit-dextrin outer branches.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Debranching enzyme deficiency produces limit dextrin; branching enzyme deficiency produces long poorly soluble chains.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What pattern suggests McArdle disease?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Exercise cramps/myoglobinuria with failure of lactate to rise because muscle phosphorylase is deficient.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glycogen architecture and liver–muscle functional contrast
concepts.summary: Glycogen is a cytosolic, highly branched glucose polymer optimized for rapid mobilization; liver supports blood glucose while muscle supports contraction.
keyPoints: Glucose residues are linked alpha-1,4 in chains and alpha-1,6 at branch points roughly every 8-12 residues.
A glycogen particle has one reducing end attached to glycogenin and many nonreducing ends where synthase and phosphorylase act simultaneously.
Branching increases solubility and the number of accessible nonreducing ends, accelerating both synthesis and degradation.
Liver glycogen buffers blood glucose; muscle glycogen is a local fuel because muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase.
Glycogen is stored in cytosolic granules containing substrate plus synthetic, degradative, and regulatory enzymes.
Architecture is function: branching is not decorative, it creates parallel reaction sites and prevents long-chain precipitation.
Liver and muscle use much of the same machinery but differ in hormonal receptors, glucose 6-phosphatase, and physiologic purpose.
examTraps: The reducing end is not the main site of chain elongation.
Muscle glycogen does not directly maintain plasma glucose.

retrievalPrompts.answer: It increases solubility and creates many nonreducing ends for parallel enzyme action.

retrievalPrompts.answer: Liver contains glucose 6-phosphatase and exports free glucose; muscle does not.
