Contrast liver and muscle glycogen by physiologic purpose and ability to release glucose.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Glycogen synthase and branching enzyme
concepts.summary: Glycogen synthase extends alpha-1,4 chains at nonreducing ends; branching enzyme transfers a terminal block to create alpha-1,6 branches.
keyPoints: Glycogen synthase transfers glucose from UDP-glucose to a nonreducing end and makes alpha-1,4 bonds.
The branching enzyme (amylo-alpha(1→4) to alpha(1→6) transglycosylase) moves a terminal chain segment to an internal C6 hydroxyl.
A transferred block contains several residues and must be placed far enough from an existing branch to preserve enzyme access.
Branching raises solubility and increases sites for rapid synthase/phosphorylase action.
Glycogen synthase is most active when dephosphorylated; glucose 6-phosphate allosterically activates even the less-active phosphorylated b form.
Synthesis alternates elongation and branch creation; branching enzyme does not add new glucose from UDP-glucose.
Covalent and allosteric regulation work together: phosphorylation sets baseline activity, while glucose 6-phosphate reports substrate abundance.
examTraps: Branching enzyme creates alpha-1,6, not alpha-1,4, bonds.
Glycogen synthase acts at nonreducing ends and cannot initiate a chain.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do synthase and branching enzyme divide labor?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Synthase adds UDP-glucose-derived residues via alpha-1,4 bonds; branching enzyme relocates a chain segment and forms an alpha-1,6 bond.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which form of glycogen synthase is more active?
retrievalPrompts.answer: The dephosphorylated a form; G6P can activate the phosphorylated b form allosterically.

objectives.text: Differentiate chain elongation from branch creation by donor, bond, and reaction mechanism.
Predict synthase activity from phosphorylation state and glucose 6-phosphate.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: UDP-glucose activation and glycogenin priming
concepts.summary: Glucose 6-phosphate is rearranged and activated as UDP-glucose; glycogenin autoglucosylation supplies the primer that glycogen synthase cannot create.
keyPoints: Phosphoglucomutase reversibly interconverts glucose 6-phosphate and glucose 1-phosphate through a glucose 1,6-bisphosphate intermediate.
UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase forms UDP-glucose from glucose 1-phosphate and UTP; pyrophosphate hydrolysis drives the reaction.
Glycogenin autoglucosylates a tyrosine hydroxyl using UDP-glucose and builds a short alpha-1,4 primer.
Glycogen synthase can elongate an existing chain but cannot initiate glycogen de novo.
UDP released during elongation is converted back to UTP at an ATP cost, so glycogen synthesis consumes high-energy phosphate.
Distinguish glucose activation from polymer elongation: UDP-glucose formation selects and energizes the glucosyl donor before synthase acts.
Glycogenin remains at the particle core and defines the single reducing end.
examTraps: UDP-glucose, not free glucose or glucose 6-phosphate, is the direct donor.
Glycogen synthase needs a primer; glycogenin initiates the particle.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How is glucose activated for glycogen synthesis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: G1P + UTP forms UDP-glucose, driven by PPi hydrolysis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does glycogenin contribute?
retrievalPrompts.answer: A self-glucosylated tyrosine-linked primer of short alpha-1,4 glucose residues.

objectives.text: Trace glucose 6-phosphate through glucose 1-phosphate to UDP-glucose and account for UTP use.
Explain why glycogenin is required before glycogen synthase can elongate a chain.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Essential fructosuria and hereditary fructose intolerance
concepts.summary: Fructokinase deficiency is benign, whereas aldolase B deficiency traps phosphate as fructose 1-phosphate and causes post-fructose hepatic energy failure.
keyPoints: Essential fructosuria is an autosomal-recessive fructokinase deficiency with benign fructose in blood/urine; hexokinase metabolizes some fructose.
Hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) is aldolase B deficiency and presents after fructose/sucrose intake with vomiting, hypoglycemia, jaundice, and possible liver/renal injury.
Fructose 1-phosphate accumulation traps phosphate and lowers ATP, inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Treatment is strict avoidance of fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol; early dietary treatment prevents ongoing organ injury.
HFI should be distinguished from fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency, a gluconeogenic defect not caused specifically by dietary fructose exposure.
The timing of symptoms is diagnostic: HFI appears when fruit juice, sucrose-containing foods, or formulas introduce fructose.
Reducing sugar in urine with normal glucose and no illness suggests benign essential fructosuria.
examTraps: HFI is aldolase B deficiency, not fructokinase deficiency.
Sorbitol must also be avoided because it can be converted to fructose.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does aldolase B deficiency cause hypoglycemia?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Fructose 1-phosphate traps phosphate and depletes ATP, impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do management and severity differ from essential fructosuria?
retrievalPrompts.answer: HFI requires avoidance of fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol; essential fructosuria is benign and generally needs no treatment.

objectives.text: Differentiate fructokinase deficiency from aldolase B deficiency by metabolite, symptoms, and mechanism.
Select appropriate dietary treatment for HFI and explain why sorbitol is excluded.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Dietary fructose sources, transport, and hepatic entry
concepts.summary: Dietary fructose from sucrose, fruit, and high-fructose sweeteners is transported to liver, where fructokinase channels it rapidly to fructose 1-phosphate.
keyPoints: Sucrose hydrolysis yields glucose plus fructose; fructose is absorbed through GLUT5 apically and leaves enterocytes through basolateral GLUT2.
Hepatic fructokinase has low Km and high Vmax and phosphorylates fructose at carbon 1 using ATP.
Hexokinase can phosphorylate fructose to fructose 6-phosphate in extrahepatic tissues, but glucose competitively limits this minor route.
Aldolase B cleaves fructose 1-phosphate to DHAP and glyceraldehyde; triokinase converts glyceraldehyde to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.
Entry below PFK-1 bypasses glycolysis's principal rate-limiting step and can drive unregulated triose-phosphate/lipid synthesis after large fructose loads.
Track the carbon position: fructokinase makes fructose 1-phosphate, whereas hexokinase makes fructose 6-phosphate.
The liver pathway's kinetic speed and PFK-1 bypass explain metabolic consequences; they are not evidence that fructose yields more ATP per molecule.
examTraps: Fructokinase is not PFK-1.
Sucrose contains glucose and fructose, whereas lactose contains glucose and galactose.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does hepatic fructose reach glycolytic intermediates?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Fructokinase → fructose 1-phosphate; aldolase B → DHAP + glyceraldehyde; triokinase → glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why can fructose favor TAG synthesis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It enters as triose phosphates below PFK-1, allowing relatively unregulated carbon flux to glycerol 3-phosphate and acetyl-CoA.

objectives.text: Trace dietary fructose from sucrose/intestinal transport to hepatic triose phosphates and compare fructokinase with hexokinase.
Explain why hepatic fructose bypasses PFK-1 and can favor TAG synthesis.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Galactokinase deficiency and classic galactosemia
concepts.summary: Galactokinase deficiency mainly produces cataracts; GALT deficiency produces systemic toxicity from galactose 1-phosphate and galactitol after milk exposure.
keyPoints: Galactokinase deficiency causes galactose accumulation and galactitol-dependent infantile cataracts but usually lacks severe liver disease.
Classic galactosemia is GALT deficiency, presenting after lactose feeding with vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis risk.
Aldose reductase converts excess galactose to galactitol in the lens; galactitol is osmotically active and poorly metabolized.
Treatment removes lactose/galactose, but endogenous galactose production means long-term complications may still occur.
Newborn screening and rapid dietary exclusion prevent acute liver failure and infection risk.
Both disorders can cause cataracts, so systemic liver/sepsis features and galactose 1-phosphate accumulation point toward GALT deficiency.
Milk exposure introduces lactose, whose hydrolysis releases galactose; symptoms begin early in classic galactosemia.
examTraps: Cataracts alone do not prove classic galactosemia.
Avoidance reduces exogenous galactose but does not stop endogenous UDP-galactose formation.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do galactokinase and GALT deficiencies differ clinically?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Galactokinase deficiency is mainly cataracts; GALT deficiency causes systemic neonatal illness plus cataracts.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What creates the cataract?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Aldose reductase converts galactose to osmotically trapped galactitol in the lens.

objectives.text: Differentiate galactokinase deficiency from GALT deficiency by metabolite and phenotype.
Explain galactitol formation and cataract pathogenesis in galactose disorders.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Leloir pathway and UDP-sugar interconversion
concepts.summary: Galactose is trapped as galactose 1-phosphate and exchanged with UDP-glucose so its carbon becomes glucose 1-phosphate while UDP-galactose is recycled.
keyPoints: Galactokinase uses ATP to form galactose 1-phosphate.
Galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) transfers UDP from UDP-glucose to galactose 1-phosphate, producing UDP-galactose and glucose 1-phosphate.
UDP-hexose 4-epimerase reversibly interconverts UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose.
Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose 1-phosphate to glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis or glycogen metabolism.
UDP-galactose also supplies biosynthesis of lactose, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and glycosaminoglycans; endogenous epimerization means galactose is not nutritionally essential.
The uridyltransferase reaction exchanges sugar phosphates; it does not simply hydrolyze UDP-glucose.
Keep substrate names explicit: GALT deficiency accumulates galactose 1-phosphate, not fructose 1-phosphate.
examTraps: Galactokinase precedes GALT.
UDP-hexose epimerase acts on UDP sugars, not free galactose/glucose.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the products of the GALT reaction?
retrievalPrompts.answer: UDP-galactose and glucose 1-phosphate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is dietary galactose not essential?
retrievalPrompts.answer: UDP-glucose can be epimerized to UDP-galactose for biosynthesis.

objectives.text: Trace galactose through galactokinase, GALT, UDP-hexose epimerase, and phosphoglucomutase.
Explain how UDP-galactose supports biosynthesis even without dietary galactose.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Lactose synthase and lactation-specific substrate selection
concepts.summary: In lactating mammary gland, alpha-lactalbumin modifies galactosyltransferase specificity so UDP-galactose is transferred to glucose to form lactose.
keyPoints: Lactose is galactose beta-1,4 linked to glucose and is synthesized in the Golgi of lactating mammary epithelium.
Lactose synthase comprises galactosyltransferase plus alpha-lactalbumin; alpha-lactalbumin lowers the enzyme's Km for glucose.
Without alpha-lactalbumin, galactosyltransferase normally transfers galactose to N-acetylglucosamine in glycoprotein synthesis.
Prolactin induces alpha-lactalbumin after parturition, redirecting enzyme specificity toward lactose production.
UDP-galactose donates galactose and glucose is the acceptor; UDP is released.
This is a classic regulatory-subunit concept: the catalytic protein already exists, but association with a tissue-specific modifier changes substrate affinity and physiologic function.
Do not confuse lactose synthesis with intestinal lactase hydrolysis.
examTraps: Alpha-lactalbumin is a modifier, not the galactose donor.
Lactose contains galactose plus glucose; sucrose contains fructose plus glucose.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What makes lactose synthase lactation specific?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Prolactin-induced alpha-lactalbumin associates with galactosyltransferase and lowers its Km for glucose.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the donor and acceptor?
retrievalPrompts.answer: UDP-galactose is the galactosyl donor and glucose is the acceptor.

objectives.text: State lactose composition, donor, acceptor, enzyme components, compartment, and prolactin response.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Mannose entry and the sorbitol/polyol pathway
concepts.summary: Mannose enters glycolysis as fructose 6-phosphate, while aldose reductase and sorbitol dehydrogenase create a tissue-dependent glucose-to-fructose polyol route.
keyPoints: Hexokinase converts mannose to mannose 6-phosphate; phosphomannose isomerase converts it to fructose 6-phosphate.
Aldose reductase uses NADPH to reduce glucose to sorbitol and is present in lens, retina, Schwann cells, kidney, ovaries, and seminal vesicles.
Sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidizes sorbitol to fructose using NAD+ and is prominent in liver, ovaries, and seminal vesicles.
Lens, retina, kidney, and Schwann cells have little sorbitol dehydrogenase; hyperglycemia therefore causes osmotic sorbitol accumulation and oxidative stress.
The polyol pathway supplies fructose to seminal fluid but contributes to diabetic cataract, retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy in vulnerable tissues.
Two mechanisms can coexist in hyperglycemic injury: osmotic swelling from trapped sorbitol and NADPH consumption that weakens antioxidant defense.
Tissue expression of the second enzyme determines whether sorbitol accumulates or is converted onward to fructose.
examTraps: Aldose reductase consumes NADPH; it does not generate NADH.
Mannose enters as F6P, not fructose 1-phosphate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does sorbitol accumulate in the lens during hyperglycemia?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Aldose reductase makes sorbitol, but little sorbitol dehydrogenase is present to remove it.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does mannose enter glycolysis?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Mannose → mannose 6-phosphate → fructose 6-phosphate.

objectives.text: Trace mannose into glycolysis and distinguish its intermediates from fructose metabolism.
Predict tissue-specific sorbitol accumulation from aldose-reductase/sorbitol-dehydrogenase expression and redox cofactors.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Chylomicron structure, apoB-48/MTP assembly, and lymphatic route
concepts.summary: Enterocytes package re-esterified long-chain lipids into apoB-48-containing chylomicrons, which leave by lymph before reaching blood.
keyPoints: The hydrophobic core contains TAG and cholesteryl ester; the surface monolayer contains phospholipid, free cholesterol, and apolipoproteins.
ApoB-48 is the essential structural apolipoprotein made in intestine and remains with the particle throughout its life.
Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) loads lipid onto nascent apoB-48 in the ER; loss of MTP prevents secretion of intestinal apoB-containing particles.
Particles mature through Golgi, are exocytosed into lacteals, travel through lymph/thoracic duct, and enter systemic blood at the left subclavian vein.
After entering blood, nascent chylomicrons obtain apoC-II and apoE from HDL.
A monolayer, not bilayer, surrounds a neutral-lipid core because the particle has only one aqueous interface.
The lymphatic detour prevents immediate portal delivery of large long-chain TAG particles.
examTraps: Albumin carries free fatty acids, not intact chylomicrons.
ApoB-48 is structural; apoC-II activates LPL and apoE mediates remnant uptake.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the core and surface components of a chylomicron?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Core: TAG and cholesteryl ester; surface: phospholipid, free cholesterol, and apolipoproteins.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What roles do apoB-48 and MTP play?
retrievalPrompts.answer: ApoB-48 scaffolds the particle; MTP transfers lipid onto nascent apoB during assembly.

objectives.text: Infer chylomicron structure from lipid polarity and trace enterocyte-to-blood transport through lymph.
Distinguish apoB-48/MTP assembly roles from apoC-II and apoE functions acquired in plasma.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Duodenal emulsification and bile-salt amphipathicity
concepts.summary: Peristalsis and amphipathic bile salts subdivide large lipid droplets, increasing enzyme-accessible surface without hydrolyzing ester bonds.
keyPoints: Gastric mixing creates a coarse emulsion; the major emulsification occurs in duodenum through intestinal motility plus bile salts.
Bile salts have hydrophobic and hydrophilic faces, adsorb at oil–water interfaces, and prevent small droplets from recoalescing.
Smaller droplets have greater surface-area-to-volume ratio, improving access for water-soluble pancreatic enzymes.
Emulsification is physical dispersion, distinct from enzymatic hydrolysis and from mixed-micelle formation after digestion.
Bile salts are later reabsorbed predominantly in terminal ileum and undergo enterohepatic circulation; less than 5% are normally lost in feces.
Follow the sequence: emulsified droplet is the substrate platform for enzymes; mixed micelles are later carriers of hydrolysis products through the unstirred layer.
Loss of terminal ileum reduces bile-salt pool and can cause fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.
examTraps: Bile salts do not hydrolyze TAG.
Emulsified droplets and mixed micelles are not interchangeable structures.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What is the mechanistic benefit of emulsification?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It increases lipid–water interface area for pancreatic enzyme action.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What happens to bile salts after micellar delivery?
retrievalPrompts.answer: They remain in the lumen and are reabsorbed mainly in terminal ileum for enterohepatic recycling.

objectives.text: Explain how motility and amphipathic bile salts emulsify lipid and increase enzyme access.
Differentiate droplets from micelles and predict the effect of terminal-ileal bile-salt loss.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Enterocyte activation and re-esterification of absorbed lipids
concepts.summary: Long-chain fatty acids are activated to acyl-CoA and used to resynthesize TAG, cholesteryl ester, and phospholipid in enterocyte smooth ER.
keyPoints: Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase (thiokinase) activates fatty acids using ATP to AMP + PPi, costing two high-energy phosphate bonds.
The dominant intestinal TAG pathway acylates 2-monoacylglycerol to diacylglycerol and then TAG.
Cholesterol is re-esterified by acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT).
Lysophospholipids are reacylated to phospholipids; these reactions occur predominantly in smooth ER.
Re-esterification re-creates hydrophobic storage/transport lipids from the more absorbable hydrolysis products.
Digestion and absorption temporarily dismantle esterified lipids; the enterocyte reconstructs them before systemic transport.
ATP-to-AMP activation is energetically equivalent to using two ATP phosphate bonds because PPi is hydrolyzed.
examTraps: Pancreatic lipase acts in the lumen; ACAT and acyltransferases act inside enterocytes.
ACAT esterifies cholesterol; cholesterol esterase hydrolyzes cholesteryl ester.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What happens to long-chain fatty acids after enterocyte uptake?
retrievalPrompts.answer: They are activated to acyl-CoA and used to re-esterify TAG, cholesterol, and phospholipid.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which enzyme re-esterifies cholesterol?
retrievalPrompts.answer: ACAT uses fatty acyl-CoA to form cholesteryl ester.

objectives.text: Explain ATP-dependent fatty-acid activation and resynthesis of TAG/phospholipid in enterocyte ER.
Distinguish ACAT-mediated cholesterol re-esterification from luminal cholesterol-ester hydrolysis.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Fates of chylomicron-derived fatty acids and glycerol
concepts.summary: LPL products separate: fatty acids enter local muscle/adipose pathways, while glycerol travels to liver for phosphorylation and carbohydrate/lipid metabolism.
keyPoints: Free fatty acids enter nearby cells; muscle can activate and oxidize them, whereas adipose can activate and re-esterify them into TAG.
Some fatty acids remain albumin bound in blood if not immediately taken up.
Adipocytes essentially lack glycerol kinase, so LPL-derived glycerol is transported to liver.
Hepatic glycerol kinase makes glycerol 3-phosphate, which can become DHAP for glycolysis/gluconeogenesis or support TAG synthesis.
A single LPL reaction coordinates fuel delivery but does not dictate fate: nearby muscle can oxidize fatty acids, while adipose can re-esterify them.
The lack of adipose glycerol kinase explains why glycerol travels to liver rather than being efficiently phosphorylated in adipose tissue.
examTraps: Glycerol is not phosphorylated primarily in adipose tissue.
LPL-derived fatty acids do not all go to liver.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why does glycerol travel to liver after LPL action?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Adipose essentially lacks glycerol kinase; liver phosphorylates glycerol for gluconeogenesis, glycolysis, or TAG synthesis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How do the immediate fates of chylomicron-derived fatty acids differ between muscle and adipose?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Muscle can activate and oxidize them for energy, whereas adipose can activate and re-esterify them into TAG.

objectives.text: Compare fatty-acid fate in muscle and adipose and explain albumin carriage.
Trace glycerol to hepatic glycerol 3-phosphate/DHAP and explain adipose's limited glycerol recycling.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: CCK and secretin control of lipid digestion
concepts.summary: Fat/protein products trigger CCK, while acidic chyme triggers secretin; together they deliver enzymes, bile, and bicarbonate and slow gastric emptying.
keyPoints: Lipids and partially digested proteins in lower duodenum/jejunum stimulate cholecystokinin release from mucosal cells.
CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic digestive-enzyme secretion and slows gastric emptying.
Acidic chyme stimulates secretin release from intestinal cells.
Secretin promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion, neutralizing acid and providing a favorable pH for pancreatic enzymes.
The two hormones are complementary: CCK supplies enzymes/bile delivery, secretin supplies alkaline fluid.
Choose the hormone by luminal stimulus and effector: fat/amino acids → CCK → enzymes and gallbladder; acid → secretin → bicarbonate.
Neutralization protects duodenal mucosa and removes acid inhibition of pancreatic enzyme activity.
examTraps: Secretin does not chiefly contract the gallbladder.
CCK stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion, whereas secretin emphasizes bicarbonate-rich fluid.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What distinguishes CCK from secretin?
retrievalPrompts.answer: CCK responds to fat/protein and drives enzymes/gallbladder contraction; secretin responds to acid and drives bicarbonate.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is slowing gastric emptying useful after fat enters duodenum?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It matches delivery rate to the slower capacity for lipid emulsification and digestion.

objectives.text: Predict CCK/secretin release and their pancreatic, biliary, and gastric effects from duodenal contents.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Lipid properties, physiologic roles, and dietary composition
concepts.summary: Hydrophobic lipids require compartmentation or protein transport and serve as fuels, membranes, insulation, and signaling precursors; dietary TAG is quantitatively dominant.
keyPoints: Hydrophobicity drives storage in droplets, incorporation into membranes, carriage on albumin, or packaging in lipoproteins.
Lipids provide concentrated energy, thermal/electrical insulation, membrane structure, and precursors of steroid hormones, bile acids, and eicosanoids.
More than 90% of dietary lipid is triacylglycerol; the remainder includes cholesterol, cholesteryl esters, phospholipids, and free fatty acids.
The local lecture estimates about 78 g/day, whereas Lippincott gives about 81 g/day for average U.S. intake; the numerical difference must remain source labeled.
Disordered lipid metabolism contributes to atherosclerosis, diabetes-associated dyslipidemia, and obesity.
The aqueous-solubility problem explains every later step: emulsification, enzyme access, micelles, intracellular re-esterification, and lipoprotein packaging.
Treat intake figures as source-specific descriptive values, not immutable physiology.
examTraps: Amphipathic membrane lipids are not freely soluble just because they contain a polar head group.
Do not merge the 78-g course estimate with the 81-g book figure.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why are plasma lipids protein associated?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Their hydrophobicity makes unassisted transport in aqueous plasma unfavorable.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What dominates dietary lipid mass?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Triacylglycerol, over 90%; cholesterol/esters, phospholipids, and free fatty acids comprise most of the remainder.

objectives.text: Relate lipid hydrophobicity to compartmentation, transport, membrane function, and disease.
Distinguish TAG from the principal minor dietary lipids.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Lipoprotein lipase, apoC-II, tissue delivery, and chylomicronemia
concepts.summary: Capillary-endothelial LPL hydrolyzes circulating chylomicron TAG under apoC-II control, delivering fatty acids to muscle and adipose tissue.
keyPoints: LPL is synthesized mainly in adipose and muscle and is transported to the luminal capillary endothelial surface.
ApoC-II activates LPL; chylomicrons acquire apoC-II after entering blood.
Hydrolysis releases free fatty acids and glycerol; muscle can oxidize fatty acids, whereas adipose can re-esterify them for storage.
LPL or apoC-II deficiency causes familial chylomicronemia with fasting milky plasma, severe hypertriglyceridemia, and pancreatitis risk.
Do not confuse lipoprotein lipase with hormone-sensitive lipase: LPL acts on circulating lipoprotein TAG at capillaries; HSL mobilizes stored adipose TAG intracellularly.
The same released fatty acid has tissue-dependent fate based on energy state and enzyme expression.
examTraps: ApoC-II activates LPL; apoE is the remnant-receptor ligand.
LPL acts on circulating lipoprotein TAG at capillaries; intracellular adipose lipolysis is a different process.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Where does LPL act and what activates it?
retrievalPrompts.answer: On the luminal capillary endothelium, activated by apoC-II.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What pattern suggests LPL/apoC-II deficiency?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Persistent fasting chylomicrons, milky plasma, severe TAG elevation, and pancreatitis risk.

objectives.text: Explain LPL location, apoC-II activation, products, and tissue-specific fatty-acid use.
Recognize familial chylomicronemia and distinguish it from remnant-clearance disease.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Mixed micelles, unstirred water layer, and chain-length dependence
concepts.summary: Mixed micelles solubilize hydrophobic digestion products and deliver them across the unstirred layer to enterocytes; short/medium chains can bypass this requirement.
keyPoints: Mixed micelles contain bile salts plus free fatty acids, 2-monoacylglycerol, cholesterol, lysophospholipids, and fat-soluble vitamins.
Their hydrophilic exterior and hydrophobic core solubilize products in the intestinal lumen and traverse the unstirred water layer.
Lipids leave the micelle at the brush border and enter the enterocyte; bile salts remain luminal until terminal-ileal uptake.
Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are sufficiently water soluble to enter portal blood directly, usually albumin bound, without micelles or chylomicrons.
Cholesterol absorption is relatively inefficient and can be reduced by ezetimibe.
Micelles are transport aggregates that repeatedly deliver cargo; the intact micelle is not endocytosed as one particle.
Chain length determines route: long-chain lipids are re-esterified and lymphatically exported; shorter chains go directly to portal blood.
examTraps: Bile salts generally do not enter the enterocyte together with each lipid cargo molecule.
Short/medium chains do not require chylomicron packaging.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does a mixed micelle accomplish?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It solubilizes hydrophobic products and carries them through the unstirred water layer to the brush border.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Which products bypass micelles and lymph?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids, which enter portal blood directly.

objectives.text: Identify mixed-micelle composition, structure, and absorptive function.
Predict portal versus lymphatic transport from fatty-acid chain length.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Pancreatic TAG, cholesteryl-ester, and phospholipid digestion
concepts.summary: Pancreatic enzymes convert complex lipids to absorbable products; colipase anchors lipase despite the bile-salt-coated interface.
keyPoints: Pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes TAG at sn-1 and sn-3 to yield 2-monoacylglycerol plus two free fatty acids.
Bile salts can inhibit lipase binding to droplets; trypsin-activated colipase anchors pancreatic lipase to the interface.
Cholesterol esterase hydrolyzes cholesteryl ester to cholesterol plus fatty acid and also acts on other lipid esters.
Trypsin activates prophospholipase A2; phospholipase A2 removes the sn-2 fatty acid to form lysophospholipid plus free fatty acid.
Pancreatic lipase is abundant and efficient, so significant fat malabsorption usually requires severe pancreatic insufficiency.
Enzyme specificity predicts product structure: keeping the sn-2 acyl group explains why 2-monoacylglycerol is the dominant TAG product.
Colipase solves an interface problem; it is not a digestive hydrolase.
examTraps: Colipase binds lipase/droplet, not bile salts to micelles.
Phospholipase A2 releases the sn-2, not sn-1, fatty acid.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What are the products of pancreatic lipase action on TAG?
retrievalPrompts.answer: 2-monoacylglycerol and two free fatty acids.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: Why is colipase needed?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It permits pancreatic lipase to bind the bile-salt-coated lipid droplet.

objectives.text: Match pancreatic lipase, cholesterol esterase, and phospholipase A2 to activation, substrate bonds, and products.
Explain colipase activation/function and why only severe pancreatic deficiency causes steatorrhea.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Chylomicron remnants, apoE uptake, type III disease, and steatorrhea
concepts.summary: After TAG removal, apoE directs cholesterol-rich remnants to liver; failures of digestion, bile delivery, absorption, or particle handling produce distinct lipid disorders.
keyPoints: Remnants retain apoB-48 and apoE and contain cholesteryl ester, phospholipid, fat-soluble vitamins, and residual TAG.
ApoE is the ligand for hepatic remnant receptors; receptor-mediated endocytosis is followed by lysosomal hydrolysis and component recycling.
Impaired apoE-dependent receptor binding can reduce remnant clearance and cause type III hyperlipoproteinemia with plasma remnant accumulation.
Steatorrhea means excess fecal fat, producing bulky, pale, greasy, foul stools and risk of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Causes can be organized as impaired pancreatic hydrolysis, reduced bile-salt delivery/pool, intestinal mucosal disease, or defective chylomicron assembly.
Compare chylomicronemia with type III: the former is failure to hydrolyze TAG-rich chylomicrons (LPL/apoC-II), the latter is failure to clear cholesterol-enriched remnants (apoE pathway).
Clinical localization follows the sequence of normal handling: pancreas/bile → micelle/enterocyte → chylomicron → LPL → remnant receptor.
examTraps: ApoE, not apoC-II, mediates hepatic remnant uptake.
Steatorrhea is a phenotype, not a single enzyme diagnosis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What does a chylomicron remnant contain and how is it cleared?
retrievalPrompts.answer: It retains apoB-48/apoE and cholesterol-rich lipid; apoE binds hepatic receptors for endocytosis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does type III differ from familial chylomicronemia?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Type III accumulates apoE-dependent remnants; chylomicronemia accumulates TAG-rich chylomicrons from failed LPL/apoC-II action.

objectives.text: Trace remnant composition and apoE-dependent hepatic uptake and recognize type III disease.
Localize steatorrhea to defects in pancreatic, bile-salt, mucosal, or chylomicron-assembly steps.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Source-specific dietary-lipid intake values
concepts.summary: The local lecture and Lippincott describe closely related but nonidentical population intake estimates, so the figures must remain attributed rather than blended.
keyPoints: Lippincott 6e reports approximately 81 g lipid per day for the average U.S. adult in the cited edition.
The local lipid lecture reports approximately 78 g per day in its teaching narrative.
Both sources agree that more than 90% of dietary lipid is triacylglycerol.
The numerical difference reflects source-specific descriptive data and does not alter the digestion pathway.
When a number differs between course and reference, retain both labels and answer a source-named question with that source's value.
Prioritize the stable concept—TAG predominance—over false precision unless the stem explicitly names the source.
examTraps: Do not average 78 and 81 into a fabricated compromise.
Do not present the book's population estimate as a universal daily requirement.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What figure belongs specifically to Lippincott 6e?
retrievalPrompts.answer: About 81 g/day, with more than 90% as TAG.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: What figure belongs to the local lecture?
retrievalPrompts.answer: About 78 g/day; it likewise emphasizes TAG predominance.

objectives.text: Preserve and retrieve the source-specific 81-g book estimate without conflating it with the 78-g course estimate.

concepts.subject: biochemistry
concepts.title: Gastric lipid digestion, neonates, and cystic-fibrosis pancreatic insufficiency
concepts.summary: Lingual and gastric lipases begin TAG hydrolysis at acidic pH and become especially important in neonates or pancreatic insufficiency.
keyPoints: Acid-stable lingual lipase is secreted from glands at the back of the tongue and acts mainly after reaching the stomach; gastric lipase is secreted by gastric mucosa.
Both have pH optima around 4-6 and preferentially hydrolyze TAG containing short- and medium-chain fatty acids.
They are especially important in neonates because milk fat is a major calorie source and contains short- and medium-chain fatty acids.
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal-recessive CFTR chloride-channel disease; reduced chloride secretion and increased sodium/water uptake dehydrate secretions.
Thick pancreatic secretions obstruct ducts, preventing enzymes from reaching intestine and causing maldigestion; treatment includes enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamins.
Lingual lipase is named for its source, not its main site of action. Its acid stability lets it function in the stomach.
CF malabsorption is a delivery failure of pancreatic secretions, not primary absence of enterocyte uptake machinery.
examTraps: Pancreatic lipase is not the enzyme initiating stomach digestion.
CFTR loss decreases chloride/water secretion; it does not simply increase pancreatic lipase degradation.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: When do lingual/gastric lipases matter most?
retrievalPrompts.answer: In neonates and in severe pancreatic insufficiency such as cystic fibrosis.

retrievalPrompts.prompt: How does CFTR dysfunction cause steatorrhea?
retrievalPrompts.answer: Dehydrated secretions obstruct pancreatic ducts, preventing digestive enzymes from entering the duodenum.

objectives.text: Compare lingual and gastric lipases by source, pH, substrate preference, site, and neonatal relevance.
Explain CFTR-dependent pancreatic insufficiency and select enzyme/vitamin replacement management.
